extracted.intended_audience: design patent applicants and patent practitioners (U.S.)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding, drafting, and prosecuting U.S. design patent applications with emphasis on the ornamentality requirement and how design patents differ from utility patents. Includes filing/examination expectations, disclosure/drawing rules, and common rejection grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic distinction between utility and design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility patent protects the way an article is used and works. A design patent protects the way an article looks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating which protection to seek, determine whether the inventive contribution is to the article's function (utility) or to its visual/ornamental appearance (design). Ornamentality can be in shape/configuration, surface ornamentation, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentality requirement for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A design consists of the visual ornamental characteristics embodied in, or applied to, an article of manufacture. The subject matter may relate to the configuration or shape of an article, the surface ornamentation applied to an article, or the combination of configuration and surface ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimed design must be ornamental in character; pure functionality negates design-patent eligibility. Consider whether the aspects claimed are visual/ornamental rather than dictated by utilitarian needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for ornamentality (primarily ornamental)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design must be 'primarily ornamental' — the claimed design is viewed in its entirety and the overall appearance is evaluated to determine whether it is dictated by utilitarian purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts commonly ask whether alternative designs could achieve the same function: if alternatives exist, the design is likely ornamental (and patentable); if no alternatives exist, the design is likely functional (and not patentable as a design). Always assess the overall visual impression rather than isolated features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term differences (design vs utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents: 20 years from U.S. filing date. Design patents (filed on or after May 13, 2015): 15 years from date of grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use term length when selecting protection strategy — design patents offer shorter exclusivity than utility patents but may be faster and cheaper to obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance fee requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents: maintenance fees required at 3.5, 7.5, and 11.5 years. Design patents: maintenance fees are NOT required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider long-term cost and upkeep when choosing between utility and design protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming format (single claim for design patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents: multiple claims allowed. Design patents: single claim only — typically 'The ornamental design for [article] as shown and described.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the single design claim to encompass the exact visual elements shown in the drawings and description; do not attempt multiple independent claimed designs in one application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination timing and docketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patent first action often in 18–24 months. Design patents often proceed faster and have a Rocket Docket option (since 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect quicker prosecution for design applications; use accelerated examination if early allowance is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirements (written description vs drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents require a detailed written description, claims, and drawings. Design patents are drawing-dominant with a brief written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For design applications, prioritize high-quality drawings that fully disclose the claimed ornamental aspects; keep the written description concise and focused on identifying the article and what is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated cost to grant: Utility patents $15,000–50,000+; Design patents $1,500–3,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget expectations differ markedly; design patents are typically a lower-cost option for protecting appearance-only inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual protection possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Both design and utility patents may be obtained on an article if invention resides both in its utility and ornamental appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention has both novel functional aspects and novel ornamental aspects, consider filing both types of applications (separate filings) to maximize protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirement for design patents (critical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must show all sides of the article (top, bottom, left, right, front, back, perspective). Surface lines define the design. Broken lines indicate an unclaimed environment; solid lines indicate the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because drawings are dominant in a design application, ensure completeness and clarity of all views. Insufficient drawings (not showing all views) are a common ground for rejection or objection; use solid vs broken lines correctly to delimit claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single design/embodiment requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent must claim a single design; showing multiple embodiments of a design in one application can lead to rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting multiple distinct designs in one set of drawings. If alternative ornamental embodiments are present, consider multiple applications or limit drawings so only one design is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title requirement for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The title must identify the article of manufacture (not an abstract design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a specific, descriptive title that names the article (e.g., 'ornamental design for a chair') rather than vague or abstract titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality doctrine and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a design is found to be functional it cannot be protected by a design patent. Functional aspects might be protectable by a utility patent if they meet novelty and non-obviousness requirements; trade dress protection may also be unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When functionality is alleged, evaluate (1) whether the design's appearance is necessitated by function, and (2) whether any functional aspects are better protected by a utility patent. Be aware that finding of functionality can foreclose design, utility, and trade dress remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common grounds for rejection of design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical rejections include: non-statutory subject matter (e.g., naturally occurring forms); lack of ornamentality (purely functional); anticipation by prior art design; obviousness over combinations of references; insufficient disclosure (drawings not showing all views); and showing multiple embodiments (must be single design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and address these grounds during drafting and prosecution: ensure original subject matter is ornamental, provide complete drawings, avoid multiple embodiments, and conduct prior-art searches to minimize anticipation/obviousness risks.
